{
  "frontend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement UI integration to call the server-side restore API and to surface server-determined outcomes to users. Requirements and constraints to follow exactly (frontend must not perform time-based restore-window checks locally; server judgment is authoritative):

API usage
- Provide a single user action (e.g., a Restore button) that issues a REST request to the backend restore endpoint for the resource ID. Do not attempt to compute or enforce the 7×24 window client-side. Use the canonical resource ID already used by your app.
- Use the HTTP request method and path defined by backend (coordinate on a single path). The frontend must send any authentication credentials it normally uses for protected API calls.

Success and failure handling (exact behavior mapped to HTTP status codes returned by backend):
- 200 OK (success): treat as successful restore. Refresh the resource view/list from the server (re-fetch the resource or list) to present the server’s current representation. Update UI state to reflect resource is no longer deleted.
- 204 No Content (if backend chooses this instead of 200): treat as success the same as 200; re-fetch resource/list.
- 410 Restore window expired: display a clear error to the user using the server-provided detail message. Example visible message: "Restore window expired" (use the server detail string). Disable further restore attempts for this resource until it is re-created or available again per server behavior.
- 409 Conflict (resource is not deleted): show message that the resource is not deleted and disable/hide the Restore action for that resource (or refresh UI to reflect current status by fetching resource state).
- 404 Not Found: show resource-not-found error and navigate user appropriately (e.g., back to list). Do not attempt further restore retries.
- 403 Forbidden: show authorization error and (if appropriate in your app) prompt user to sign in/obtain permissions.
- Any other 4xx/5xx: surface generic server error and offer retry after short delay.

UI/UX specifics
- Confirm modal: optional. If present, the modal should say that restore is subject to server-side 7×24h window and that server will decide. Do not show a local deadline or time calculation.
- Disable the Restore control while the request is in-flight; show spinner/disabled state.
- After a success, re-fetch (not rely on local optimistic update); present server-fetched state.

Testing and acceptance criteria (frontend):
- Unit/integration tests must assert that no client-side time arithmetic is used to allow/disallow restores.
- E2E tests must simulate backend responses for the status codes above and verify correct UI behavior for 200/204, 410 (message shown and restore disabled), 409, 404, 403.
- Verify that when server returns 410 the frontend shows exactly the server detail text provided.

Observability
- Log user-initiated restore attempts and server response status for diagnostics (do not include sensitive auth tokens in logs)."
  },
  "backend": {
    "needed": true,
    "prompt": "Implement a server-side restore operation that enforces a strict 7×24-hour (604800 seconds) restore window determined using server UTC time. Follow these exact rules and ordering; do not perform any automatic physical deletion as part of this flow.

API contract (define a single restore endpoint to implement):
- Endpoint: choose a single canonical endpoint for restore, e.g. POST /resources/{id}/restore (or the equivalent in your API platform). Document this path in the API spec so frontend can call it.
- Authentication: endpoint requires the same auth/authorization used for modifying the resource.

Behavior and checks (MUST be executed in this order):
1) Existence check: confirm the resource exists by ID.
   - If not found -> return 404 Not Found.
2) Authorization check: confirm caller is authorized to restore this resource.
   - If not authorized -> return 403 Forbidden.
3) Deletion status check: determine whether the resource is currently deleted.
   - If the resource is not marked deleted (deleted_at is NULL or equivalent) -> return 409 Conflict (resource is not deleted). Do not proceed to time checks.
4) Restore window check: compute window using server UTC time.
   - Let now_utc = current server time in UTC (use a reliable clock source; do not use local timezone offsets).
   - Let deleted_at be the resource's deletion timestamp (must be stored in UTC).
   - Compute elapsed_seconds = (now_utc - deleted_at) in seconds.
   - If elapsed_seconds < 604800 then allow restore.
   - If elapsed_seconds >= 604800 then return 410 Gone with JSON body {"detail": "Restore window expired"}.
   - Note: if deleted_at is missing or malformed, treat as not deletable; return 409 Conflict or 400 Bad Request per your API standards, but prefer 409 if the resource is logically not deleted.

Restore action
- When allowed, perform the restore operation atomically:
  - Within a transaction / atomic update: verify the resource is still deleted (to avoid race conditions), and then clear deleted_at (set to NULL) and update any status fields needed by your domain model so the resource is active again. Preserve all other fields.
  - Do not physically delete or permanently purge any data during this operation.
  - Return 200 OK with the resource representation as returned by your existing GET resource contract (i.e., same representation format), or 204 No Content if your API style prefers no body. Document which you choose in the API spec.

Responses summary (required exact status codes/messages):
- 200 OK (or 204) — success; return restored resource representation if 200.
- 410 Gone — restore window expired; response body must include JSON {"detail": "Restore window expired"}.
- 409 Conflict — resource is not deleted (do not attempt time check if resource not deleted).
- 404 Not Found — resource does not exist.
- 403 Forbidden — caller not authorized.

Other constraints
- Do not automatically physically purge/garbage-collect expired items as part of this implementation; the requirement explicitly forbids automatic physical cleanup as a side-effect of this restore logic.
- Use UTC consistently for deleted_at storage and for computing now_utc.
- Ensure race-safety: perform existence/status/time checks and the update in a transaction or use a conditional update that only clears deleted_at when deleted_at is unchanged and elapsed_seconds < 604800. If the conditional fails, re-read final state and return the appropriate error code (409/410/etc.) to the caller.

Testing and acceptance criteria (backend)
- Unit tests: cover
  - Success case: deleted_at such that now_utc - deleted_at < 604800 -> resource restored and deleted_at cleared.
  - Boundary failure: deleted_at such that now_utc - deleted_at == 604800 -> return 410 with detail exactly "Restore window expired".
  - Just-over-boundary: elapsed >= 604800 -> 410.
  - Not-deleted: deleted_at NULL -> 409.
  - Not-found -> 404.
  - Unauthorized -> 403.
- Integration tests: exercise actual endpoint with mocked clock to simulate times (use deterministic clock injection or freeze time in tests). Verify transactionality and that no physical deletion occurs.
- E2E tests: frontend should rely on these responses (see frontend acceptance tests).

Logging and monitoring
- Log restore attempts with user ID, resource ID, and outcome status code. Do not log sensitive tokens.

Documentation
- Document the endpoint, its HTTP method, expected request/response shapes, and the exact error status codes and messages (including the required 410 detail string) so frontend can implement correct handling.

Do not make any client-side time assumptions or expose client-side ways to override the server-side UTC judgment. Follow the exact ordering of checks specified above."
  }
}

My focus needs to be on valid JSON format while keeping the details tight yet clear for both backend and frontend prompts. Additionally, I'll ensure that my test cases cover boundary conditions effectively.
